British Medical Association Runs A Non-Debate On Medical Marijuana
The Prohibitionist Ignores the Fact That Patients Are Being Arrested
– Unless Court Records Are Just Anecdotal Evidence.

HEAD2HEAD

Joint Debate

(Marijuananews note: Even the BMA can’t resist the mandatory marijuana pun in its header. More substantively, the introductory sentence below does not present Robson's major point about arresting patients.)

There is anecdotal evidence that cannabis contains useful therapeutic properties. But should prescription be the next step?

Phillip Robson says denying certain patients access to the drug is inhumane.

Professor Sir Michael Rawlins says we must wait for further tests.

Phillip Robson is a Consultant Psychiatrist at Warneford Hospital, Oxford, a senior clinical lecturer and author of "Forbidden Drugs".

"To criminalise patients seeking symptom relief is absurd"

In 1998, the Lords select committee on science and technology examined in detail the scientific and medical evidence regarding the possible therapeutic use of cannabis and its derivative cannabinoids.
See
The House of Lords Press Release On Medical Marijuana; Medical, Yes; Legalization, No

The conclusion was that insufficient evidence exists to prove its therapeutic use, but cannabis almost certainly does have genuine medical applications.

Few now disagree there is ample justification to subject cannabinoids to rigorous testing through controlled research in selected clinical disorders. Trials for synthetic preparations are underway under the auspices of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society and other organisations.

The problem is the results of these trials, and any subsequent pharmaceutical and regulatory response, are several years away.

The select committee also concluded there was a need to show compassion towards patients currently risking prosecution to obtain symptom relief, and that doctors may legitimately wish to prescribe cannabis for certain conditions.

See
Chairman of the House of Lords Science and Technology Committee
Criticizes UK Government’s Rejection Of Report On Medical Marijuana
– 2 Articles With 2 of the Worst Prohibitionist Arguments

The future role of cannabinoids will be defined by the outcome of randomised clinical trials of pharmaceutically pure substances. But while we await the results, what should happen to those self-medicators who sincerely believe cannabis provides relief from their suffering?

Must they continue to expose themselves to prosecution, and to unwanted effects related to the variable purity and adulteration of black market material? To criminalise such people is absurd and inhumane.

Pending the outcome of controlled trials, it remains a matter of speculation as to whether cannabinoids are useful medicines. But for patients with certain disorders, for which conventional treatments are less than satisfactory - Aids, intractable vomiting and multiple sclerosis, for example - the balance of evidence suggests cannabis may prove beneficial with an acceptable profile of adverse effects. In terminal care, some unwanted effects - possible addiction, for example - are irrelevant.

Standardised plants cultivated under licence are now available.

See
UK Guidelines For Tests On Medical Marijuana To Be Set Today;
Muddled Reporting On Muddled "Experts" -- 2 Articles

Selection of genotype and sophisticated control of growing conditions can generate a plant extract with a purity equal to that of synthetic products. Oral administration is unreliable, but advances in aerosol and vaporiser technology make smoking the drug redundant.

See
Counterblaste to DEA: Fallacious Pharmacology.
"The contention that smoking cannot possibly be an acceptable route for the administration
of a therapeutic substance is morality dressed up as science." by Peter Webster

Patients could be asked for written informed consent to receive cannabis, using the format proposed by the Royal College of Physicians for clinical research. The form could emphasise that beneficial effects remain unproven, and list possible unwanted effects. Doctors could be made aware of exclusions, contra-indications and special precautions, as with any new drug.
(Marijuananews note: Ironically, none of these precautions are required for the use of drugs that are known to be dangerous. In fact, some former? UK users of tranquilizers are suing because they were not warned about their potential for addiction.)

See
UK Victims of Tranquilizers Urge That "Far Safer" Medical Cannabis Be Made Available -- IoS
"More people died from benzodiazepine usage than from such drugs as heroin and cocaine."

Doctors can be trusted to make sensible judgements about risks and benefits. Patients should not become casualties of the war on drugs.

Professor Sir Michael Rawlins is professor of clinical pharmacology at the University of Newcastle, chairman of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, chairman of the National Institute for Clinical Excellence and a former chairman of the Committee on Safety of Medicines.

"Anecdotal evidence forms a terrible basis for clinical practice"

(Marijuananews note: If this "debate were taking place in public, surely someone would demand that Rawlins answer the first point raised by Robson: "To criminalise patients seeking symptom relief is absurd."
See

Instead, Rawlins pretends that arrests are not happening. This is bad science and worse medicine. To paraphrase Oscar Wilde, if this is the way British medicine treats its patients, it doesn’t deserve to have any!

The one thing that Rawlins proves conclusively is that organized medicine should not be given control over access to cannabis, and they should certainly not be allowed to lock up people who decline to take their advice.)

Many modern medicines such as quinine, morphine and digoxin - to name a few - have their origins as herbal products. They have been shown to possess useful therapeutic properties - not from anecdote but from properly conducted clinical trials.

(Marijuananews note: What odd examples. All of these drugs were in use long before the present control regime was implemented. Moreover, cannabis was a part of the pharmacopoeia in the UK until the 1970s because it had long been used in medicine. It was removed for political, not scientific reasons.

Moreover, the control procedures for new drugs were created to protect patients from unscrupulous pharmaceutical companies and incompetent doctors. They were not created to persecute patients and leave them at the mercy of unscrupulous pharmaceutical companies and incompetent doctors, which is precisely what is happening.)

For cannabis or any of its components to be available as a medicine, there needs to be a product that satisfies three criteria: it must be of appropriate quality, it must have been proved effective, and it must be safe. At present, none of these criteria can be met.
(Marijuananews note: It is odd that someone who claims expertise in pharmacology would say that cannabis does not meet the criteria for safety. He must surely know that safety is a relative concept, and that cannabis is far safer than most drugs sold over the counter without a doctor’s prescription, and certainly safer than most commonly prescribed drugs.)

See
The Lancet Reports That Thousands Are Killed In Accidents Caused By Tranquilizers
and
Painkillers Put Millions At Risk Of Ulcers; Hospitalize 76,000 & Kill 7,600 Annually; One That Doesn’t Kill Is Illegal
and
Adverse Pharmaceutical Reactions Major Cause of Death; Marijuana Does Not Kill But Must Be Approved By FDA?
and
Forbes Data: "What you don't know can kill you." Which Drugs Kill the Most People?
and
Deadly Drug Sold by Founder of Partnership for A Drug-Free America, Says Forbes

Defining the quality of medicinal products of herbal origin is not easy.

Most contain numerous chemicals. Their relative contributions to the therapeutic activity of the finished product is unclear. It is usually necessary, therefore, to define a specification that encompasses their origins, processing and subsequent analytical tests.

Cannabis plants contain around 2,000 separate chemicals. Although some of these tetrahydrocannabinol, for example - have clear pharmacological properties, it is not known which, if any, of the plant's components have a therapeutic role. These components will vary with a variety of factors - which species is used, the climatic conditions under which it is grown, the precise details of harvesting, and the nature of the subsequent processing. Any pharmaceutical preparation of cannabis would need to control all these factors to ensure the availability of a consistent product.

(Marijuananews note: He is also ignoring the fact that it is very easy to grow standardized cannabis under controlled conditions and produce a consistent product. It is being done legally in one location in the UK and illegally and/or quasi-legally in most advanced countries.)

There are only anecdotes to support claims for the therapeutic value of cannabis.

Modern medicine has, I hope, learned the lessons of the past: that anecdotal evidence of efficacy forms a terrible basis for clinical practice.

(Marijuananews note: Nonsense! Again, clinical observation by competent, caring doctors is how we learn about the "off-label" uses of many approved drugs, and about the unexpected dangers of approved drugs. The plural of anecdote is data. There are tens of thousands of anecdotes over millenia that support the safety and efficacy of cannabis.)

Worse still is the fact that these anecdotes derive from the use of products with an unknown provenance, grown in uncontrolled conditions and subjected to indeterminate processing.

And to cap it all, we do not have the vaguest idea of an appropriate dose.
(Marijuananews note: What hubris! In fact, there is a very great range in the "appropriate" doses of most medicines. Moreover, when medicines are taken orally, there is a wide range in the rate of absorbtion for the same patient from day to day.

One of the great advantages of inhaling – including smoking – is that the patient can control the dose. After all, for most users of medical marijuana the objective is to relieve certain symptoms, which the patient is more competent to judge than a Sir Professor, or even a Drug Tsar.)

Furthermore, we have virtually no inkling of the likely safety problems hat might arise with a defined product. For cannabis does, unquestionably, possess known and potent pharmacological properties that may, or may not, play a part in its putative therapeutic effects.

(Marijuananews note: Someone should tell Rawlins that this is not a new drug. Perhaps he could ask around the campus and learn an "inkling" or two about its "likely safety.")

Those arguing for the legalisation of cannabis for medicinal purposes are, I know, good and honourable people acting with the best of motives. They should, though, think with their heads rather than their hearts.

(Marijuananews note: Yes, there is nothing worse than a doctor who actually cares that the patients feel better, as opposed to the proper "scientific method!" They simply do not understand that patients exist for medicine, rather than medicine existing for the patients.

Actually, there are number medicines, most notably aspirin, that have long been used without understanding how they work.)

We must all await the results of the clinical trials by the Royal Pharmaceutical Society, using a product with a well-defined specification. Only then will the debate move on.

(Marijuananews note: How bravely he endures the pain of others! I would like to propose that Rawlins be locked up in British jail to study the therapeutic benefits of being arrested. Unfortunately, this wouldn’t be a "double-blind" test, inasmuch as he would almost certainly know that he was in jail.

Of course, people suffering pain and nausea also tend to notice when they stop hurting or vomiting.

Rawlins might then explain why his subjective objections to being in jail were less anecdotal than the patients’ observations that they had stopped vomiting.)
See
Study Faults Pain Treatment In Cancer Patients; "Most doctors are not well trained to manage pain." Just Our Lives
